References / Signage / 459

Roto-Sphere sign, Joe’s Liquors, Memphis

A spinning “Sputnik” sign from Warren Milks’s Roto-Sphere series of 1960–71: a red ball with sixteen colored spikes over a zigzag arrow and a “JOE’S” box.

Source
Library of Congress: Carol M. Highsmith, Colorful space satellite-like sign for Joe’s Restaurant in Memphis, Tennessee, 2021
Creator
Warren Milks (Roto-Sphere)
Made
Roto-Spheres made 1960–1971; this one shown in a 1962 grand-opening advertisement (Roadside Architecture); restored 1999; photographed 14 October 2021
Style
Googie (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Roadside, playful, futuristic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected Carol M. Highsmith’s 2021 photograph, Library of Congress LC-DIG-highsm-68164, 683 × 1024 px, in a scratchpad. Not stored. The Library of Congress title says “Joe’s Restaurant”; the sign and the Roadside Architecture account identify the business as Joe’s Liquors (now Joe’s Wines & Liquor).
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Roadside Architecture: Warren Milks made about 234 Roto-Spheres at his sign shop in Bossier City, Louisiana, from 1960 to 1971. Each has sixteen eight-foot aluminum spikes outlined in neon, and a motor turns the ball and its counter-rotating halves. The Memphis store’s grand-opening advertisement called it “the Sign of the Sputnik”; the owners raised $12,000 to restore it in 1999. Roadside Architecture: Roto-Spheres.

The Daily Memphian reports that Roto-Spheres were not, according to historians, inspired by Sputnik, although locals call the sign “the Sputnik.” Daily Memphian.

Observed

  • A glossy red ball sits on a white pole; long tapering spikes radiate from it in all directions, each a different color: yellow, red, blue, green, teal, white, and orange.
  • Each spike is edged with a thin line of tube along its length.
  • Below the ball, a yellow-orange arrow bent into a zigzag points down to the box sign.
  • The box sign reads “JOE’S” in white capitals on a black panel with a red corner block.
  • The ground is a cloudy gray-blue sky; the neon is not lit.

Why it belongs

Whatever its maker intended, the sign reads as the style’s starburst-satellite: a central sphere with radiating rays in many saturated colors.

The zigzag arrow is a second Googie motif, the lightning bolt or boomerang that directs the driver’s eye.

Borrow

Use a central dot with radiating spikes of different colors as a badge or a loading mark.

Use a bent zigzag arrow to point from a heading to an action.
